lessons.title: Consonant to vowel linking
lessons.explain: When a word ends in a consonant and the next starts with a vowel, join them into one sound group.
points: The consonant becomes the start of the next word.

lessons.title: Vowel linking and intrusive sounds
lessons.explain: Two vowels meeting need a small bridge: /w/, /j/ or /r/ appears naturally.

items.note: Intrusive /r/ is common in British English.

lessons.title: Elision: sounds disappear
lessons.explain: In fast speech some sounds simply drop out, especially /t/ and /d/ between consonants.

lessons.title: Assimilation: sounds change
lessons.explain: A sound can change to match the next one, so the mouth moves less.

lessons.title: Contractions
lessons.explain: Natural spoken English uses contractions almost everywhere. Full forms sound formal or emphatic.

lessons.title: Weak forms
lessons.explain: Small grammar words lose their full vowel and become a schwa when they are not stressed.

lessons.title: Linking identical consonants
lessons.explain: When one word ends and the next begins with the same consonant sound, don't say it twice — hold it once, a little longer.

lessons.title: Linking /r/ in British English
lessons.explain: In non-rhotic British English, a silent final 'r' becomes pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel.

lessons.title: Reduced auxiliary verbs in questions
lessons.explain: Auxiliary verbs at the start of questions often reduce heavily in fast, casual speech.

lessons.title: Linking across three-word phrases
lessons.explain: Longer phrases link across every word boundary, not just the first pair — practise the whole chain.

lessons.title: Connected speech with 'going to'
lessons.explain: 'Going to' before a verb almost always links and reduces in natural speech.

items.text: What are you going to do?

lessons.title: Connected speech in fast greetings
lessons.explain: Very common greeting phrases are almost always run together in natural speech.

lessons.title: Linking with plural and possessive 's'
lessons.explain: The final 's' sound links smoothly into the next word's vowel, just like any other consonant.

lessons.title: Practice: a fast connected-speech paragraph
lessons.explain: Put it all together — link, reduce and contract naturally across a whole mini-paragraph.

items.text: I was gonna call you, but I didn't have time — I'll try to get in touch later on, okay?

lessons.title: H-dropping in weak pronouns
lessons.explain: Unstressed 'him', 'her' and 'his' often drop the /h/ sound completely and link to the word before.

lessons.title: Glottal stop replacing /t/
lessons.explain: Before certain consonants, /t/ is often replaced with a quick catch in the throat instead of a clear tongue-tap.

lessons.title: Linking -ing forms into the next vowel
lessons.explain: An -ing verb ending in a consonant sound links smoothly into a following vowel, just like any other word-final consonant.

lessons.title: Connected speech in dates
lessons.explain: Dates link and reduce heavily in natural speech — 'of' almost disappears.

lessons.title: Connected speech with modal + have
lessons.explain: Modal verbs followed by 'have' link and reduce so heavily that 'have' sounds like 'of' to many learners — that's just how it's linked, not actually spelled that way.

lessons.title: Connected speech in weather talk
lessons.explain: Common weather phrases link smoothly across word boundaries just like any other everyday speech.

lessons.title: Linking in business phone phrases
lessons.explain: Common office phone phrases link naturally across word boundaries — practise them as whole chunks.

lessons.title: Connected speech practice: a second fast paragraph
lessons.explain: A second full-paragraph challenge — link, reduce and contract across the whole thing.

items.text: I would've told you sooner, but I kinda forgot — I guess I've had a lot going on lately.

lessons.title: Linking with 'a lot of'
lessons.explain: 'A lot of' is one of the most common linked phrases in English — practise it as a single unit.

items.text: I have a lot of work today.

lessons.title: Connected speech in song lyrics
lessons.explain: Song lyrics are full of natural connected speech — great, memorable practice material.

items.text: Don't you wanna dance with somebody?

lessons.title: Reduced 'because' in casual speech
lessons.explain: 'Because' commonly reduces to 'cause' or 'cuz' in relaxed conversation, and links straight into the next word.

items.text: I'm tired because I stayed up late.

lessons.title: Linking with plural verb forms
lessons.explain: Verb endings link into the next word exactly the same way noun endings do.

lessons.title: Connected speech across a short dialogue
lessons.explain: Real conversation links across every turn, not just within one speaker's sentence.

items.text: A: Wanna grab a bite? B: Yeah, gimme a sec, I'm almost done.

lessons.title: Reduced 'them' as 'em
lessons.explain: 'Them' frequently reduces to 'em (dropping the 'th') and links straight onto the verb before it.

items.text: I already gave them the news.

lessons.title: Linking with numbers before nouns
lessons.explain: Numbers link into the noun that follows exactly like any consonant-to-vowel or consonant-to-consonant pair.

lessons.title: Linking prepositions of place
lessons.explain: Common location phrases link fully across every word boundary — practise them as one chunk.

lessons.title: 'There's a' and 'there's an' linking
lessons.explain: 'There's' links tightly onto the word that follows, especially before 'a lot of'.

items.text: There's a lot of traffic today.
There's an easier way to do this.

lessons.title: Negative auxiliary linking
lessons.explain: Negative contractions link straight into the next word just like any consonant ending.

lessons.title: Linking numbers with 'and'
lessons.explain: 'And' between number parts reduces to a quick /ən/ and links both sides together.

lessons.title: Connected speech in casual excuses
lessons.explain: Excuse phrases are said fast and casually, with heavy linking and reduction.

items.text: Sorry, I gotta run, I'm late for something.
I was gonna text you but I forgot.

lessons.title: 'Of course' and 'kind of' reduced linking
lessons.explain: These extremely common phrases reduce and link so much they barely resemble their spelling.

items.text: It's kind of a big deal.

lessons.title: Connected speech in fast sports commentary
lessons.explain: Live commentary links almost every word together at high speed — great advanced listening/speaking practice.

items.text: He's got it, he's through, and he scores!

lessons.title: Linking with 'going to have to'
lessons.explain: This whole obligation phrase links and reduces into a single fast chunk in natural speech.

items.text: We're going to have to reschedule.
I'm gonna have to think about it.

lessons.title: Casual 'your' reduced to 'yer'
lessons.explain: Unstressed 'your' often reduces to a quick 'yer' sound and links onto the next word.

lessons.title: Connected speech in polite offers
lessons.explain: Everyday offer phrases link smoothly across the whole sentence.

items.text: Do you want a cup of coffee?

lessons.title: Linking with 'used to' in narration
lessons.explain: 'Used to' links tightly and reduces when telling stories about the past.

items.text: I used to live in Paris.
We used to go there every summer.
items.pattern: We yoosta go there every summer.

lessons.title: Connected speech with double consonants across words
lessons.explain: When a word ends and the next begins with a similar (not identical) sound, they still often blend rather than being said as two separate sounds.

lessons.title: Connected speech in a customer-service phrase set
lessons.explain: Common service-industry phrases link naturally across the whole sentence.

items.text: Is there anything else I can help you with?
Thanks for calling, have a great day.

lessons.title: Connected speech: final review paragraph
lessons.explain: One more full-paragraph challenge pulling together linking, elision, assimilation and weak forms all at once.

items.text: I gotta admit, I kinda forgot we were supposed to meet — sorry 'bout that, I shoulda texted you.

lessons.title: Linking with 'as well as'
lessons.explain: This common linking phrase runs together into one smooth unit.

items.text: He speaks French as well as English.
It's fast as well as reliable.

lessons.title: 'Except for' reduced linking
lessons.explain: 'Except for' links tightly, with the final /t/ often barely released before 'for'.

items.text: It's ready, except for the last page.

lessons.title: Connected speech making casual plans
lessons.explain: Everyday planning phrases link and reduce heavily in relaxed conversation.

items.text: Wanna grab lunch sometime this week?
items.pattern: wanna grab lunch sometime this week

lessons.title: Linking across a movie-trailer style line
lessons.explain: Dramatic narration still links every word together — the drama is in the pacing, not gaps between words.

items.text: In a world where anything is possible, one man has to make a choice.

lessons.title: Connected speech with 'gonna' plus different pronouns
lessons.explain: 'Gonna' links the same way regardless of which pronoun comes before it.

lessons.title: Connected speech: final mixed review
lessons.explain: One last full-sentence challenge mixing linking, weak forms and reductions together.

items.text: I shoulda called you as soon as I found out, but I kinda wanted to check the details first.

lessons.title: Final mixed linking review
lessons.explain: One closing set combining consonant-vowel linking, elision and a weak form all in one line.

items.text: I want to ask about it later.
